title: ANZ Bank: DevOps modernization for core banking systems
to: Git, IBM DBB, IBM Developer for z/OS
summary: According to the case study: CI/CD framework for around 40 applications (including 3 highly critical core banking systems) and more than 1,000 application repositories in Git-based version control within 8 months; around 90% lower licensing costs compared with traditional mainframe-based SCM; hotfixes previously took approximately 4 weeks of effort to retrofit into the SCM and deploy into non-production environments; each hotfix, now deployed directly to production through the pipeline, takes an hour maximum.

title: HCSC: around 294,000 Endevor elements migrated to Git
to: Git, Jenkins, IBM DBB v3, IBM DevOps Deploy (UCD)
summary: According to the service provider’s case study: around 294,000 Endevor elements migrated to Git; 150+ applications, 100+ unique build and compilation combinations through 15 DBB language processors, replication of Endevor’s “Delete Behind” functionality, automated Db2 BINDs, without production-impacting defects.

title: Nedbank: build-to-production from hours to around 18 minutes
to: BMC AMI DevX Code Pipeline, Total Test, zAdviser; SonarQube, Azure DevOps
summary: According to the case study: build-to-production time reduced from hours to around 18 minutes; migration of around 250 mainframe developers in six months; deployment cycle reduced from 2–3 months to around 3 weeks; DORA metrics via zAdviser.

title: M&T Bank: GitLab, DBB, SonarQube and Ansible for Hogan core banking
to: GitLab (SCM + CI), IBM DBB, SonarQube, Ansible, IDz
summary: Interview with two leads: replacement of the roughly 30-year-old SCM Panvalet with Git/GitLab; DBB for builds, SonarQube, Jira/ServiceNow, Ansible for deployments via SSH. First application (Hogan) live; goal: around 100 mainframe applications on the platform.
note: Interview on a vendor community blog.

title: BMC internal team: code fix build from around 90 to around 3 minutes
to: GitHub, GitHub Actions, BMC AMI DevX Code Pipeline (Git integration)
summary: According to the case study: code-fix build time reduced from around 90 to around 3 minutes; source code stays in Git; GitHub Actions triggers Code Pipeline, which compiles only changed components.
note: Vendor reporting on its own internal team.

title: CSE (Consorzio Servizi Bancari): mainframe efficiency and compliance with BMC AMI
summary: According to the case study: replacing the previous source code management solution with BMC AMI DevX Code Pipeline created a “software factory approach”; developers can quickly deploy code or revert to a previous state.
note: Published by the vendor. The case study covers several BMC AMI products; this entry covers only its Code Pipeline paragraph.

title: Atruvia AG: Endevor to Git migration – about 3.6 million elements
publisher: IBM Expert Labs success story, available via the Q Group website
to: Bitbucket, Jenkins, IBM DBB, IBM UrbanCode Deploy, IBM Developer for z/OS Enterprise Edition
summary: According to the IBM Expert Labs success story, available via the Q Group website, the project was delivered by IBM Expert Labs with Q Group AG as main business partner. The story reports: 3,620,999 elements with up to 200 version levels, 156 Endevor element types, about 350 stakeholders, 189 application bundles migrated in phases (elements locked in Endevor after their tranche), 8 tailored courses in 52 training sessions. According to the story, the implementation project was launched in early 2023 after an MVP in 2022; the migration was finalized by September 2025 and the project was completed by the end of 2025. The latest three versions of each element went to Git; older versions were archived automatically to LDMS with Q Group’s Q-Wing.
note: Success story authored by IBM Expert Labs, published by a service provider (Q Group).

title: dwpbank: Endevor to GitLab migration in 11 months
publisher: IBM Expert Labs success story, available via the Q Group website
to: GitLab with z/OS runners, IBM DBB, IBM Wazi Deploy, VS Code-based developer interface
summary: According to the IBM Expert Labs success story, available via the Q Group website, the project was delivered by IBM Expert Labs and Q Group AG. The story reports: 181,435 elements with up to 180 version levels, 123 Endevor element types, about 120 stakeholders, 7 stages; 61 application bundles migrated to GitLab automatically by Q-Wing in tranches; latest three versions of each element migrated, older versions archived to DMS3 via Q-Wing. According to the story, the project was launched in mid-2024; the complete transformation was delivered in 11 months against a compressed schedule of 18 months, the migration was finalized by November 2025 and the project was completed by the end of 2025. The story reports that deployments went from several hours to minutes.
note: Success story authored by IBM Expert Labs, published by a service provider (Q Group); the document states the project was presented publicly at industry events including GSE (Mainz 2026).

title: Q-Wing: Endevor-to-Git migration tool and archive
to: Git (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and others); archive on Linux/Windows
summary: Product description: export rules by system, subsystem, type or an element “shopping list”; export via the Endevor API into a PDS; Git fast-import in z/OS UNIX; preserves original Endevor timestamps and authors; all versions or the last n versions incl. sync levels; delta imports into existing repositories; big-bang or iterative migration; delta-based archive for elements and versions not moved to Git; the product page names Linux or Windows for the archive. In the IBM Expert Labs success stories, Q-Wing transferred older versions to an LDMS archive (Atruvia) and a DMS3 archive (dwpbank).
note: Vendor marketing; the product page describes Endevor as the source system.

title: Mainframe AI Is Stuck at the Keyboard. The Pipeline Is Why
to: Controls and evidence inside the pipeline
summary: Reports a Techstrong PulseMeter poll of 145 mainframe software delivery professionals: 86% use AI somewhere in mainframe software delivery, 57% for code generation or developer assistance, but only about a quarter to automate deployment, security and compliance; nearly half still run manual or legacy delivery processes. Recommends finding “emailed” approvals and making policy checks, approvals and audit evidence outputs of the pipeline. Describes BMC AMI DevX Code Pipeline’s MCP server and CycloneDX SBOM generation as the featured product example.
note: Labeled “Sponsored Content” on DevOps.com; based on a webinar with BMC (Vijay Namasevi, Area VP of R&D), and the product section describes BMC’s offering.

title: Techstrong PulseMeter: The Orchestration Challenge in Mainframe Software Delivery
publisher: Techstrong PulseMeter report (Guy Currier, Futurum Group), published on DevOps.com
summary: Poll of 145 practitioners and decision-makers in mainframe software delivery. 47% report manual or legacy delivery processes in their environment. 86% use AI somewhere in mainframe delivery: 57% for code generation or developer assistance, 38% for automated testing, 35% for monitoring and incident response, 34% for build and pipeline optimization, 26% for security and compliance automation and 25% for deployment automation. 30% name support for AI-assisted delivery as a top strategic outcome.
note: Survey report; the report and its landing page state that it is sponsored by BMC.

title: PopUp Mainframe: “Getting to Git” – branching strategy, SCM history migration and pilot teams
summary: Vendor blog covering build/deploy taxonomy, branching strategies (trunk-based vs. GitHub Flow) and the migration of source plus audit history into Git. PopUp Mainframe states that its migration tools and utilities preserve the full change history (who changed what and when), support ChangeMan, Endevor and Code Pipeline, and that such repository migrations typically take a few weeks depending on structure and volume.
